Original BERT4Rec already combines random masked-item reconstruction with training examples masking only the final item, to better match appended-mask next-item inference. The paper does not specify a 50:50 mixture. Important implementation caveat: the authors’ public `gen_data.py` generates training records with `force_last=False` and evaluation records with `force_last=True`; its default training path does not explicitly add a separate last-only group, although random masking can select the last position. Thus, distinguish the paper’s stated mechanism from the released implementation. [Paper §3.6](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690#S3.SS6), [reference generator](https://github.com/FeiSun/BERT4Rec/blob/master/gen_data.py).

Loss normalization also matters. Equation (8) defines each sequence’s loss as the mean negative log-likelihood over its masked targets. The reference `run.py` instead flattens masked positions across the batch and computes `sum(weight * target_loss) / (sum(weight) + 1e-5)`, with weights one for valid targets and zero for padding. This averages valid masked targets globally; sequences with more targets contribute more weight than under an average of per-sequence means. [Reference loss](https://github.com/FeiSun/BERT4Rec/blob/master/run.py#L327-L367).

Algebraically, for two groups containing n scalar example losses each, `0.5*mean(A) + 0.5*mean(B) = mean(concat(A,B))`, with identical gradients for the same computed losses. Equal weighting therefore adds no objective change beyond constructing that balanced batch and choosing its loss normalization. Equal sequence counts do not imply equivalence to global masked-target averaging when target counts differ. For unequal group sizes, ordinary averaging requires weights `n_A/(n_A+n_B)` and `n_B/(n_A+n_B)`; separate optimizer steps also need not match one combined update.
